newsitem.title: USA: Clinton poised to celebrate with hometown backers.
newsitem.headline: Clinton poised to celebrate with hometown backers.

text.p: A festive mood gripped President Bill Clinton's hometown on Tuesday night as Clinton and his most loyal supporters followed election returns indicating he would become the first Democrat to win re-election in 52 years.

Television networks, working on exit polls, gave Democrat Clinton most of the early states called, including the plums of Florida, Pennsylvania and Illinois, suggesting he would easily defeat Republican Bob Dole.
It was still uncertain whether the 50-year-old former Arkansas governor would get a majority of the vote, although . Reform Party candidate Ross Perot was projected to finish a distant third.
As the results came in a large exhuberant crowd gathered outside Clinton's election night headquarters at the Excelsior Hotel, turning downtown Little Rock into one big party.
As many as 80,000 people were expected to congregate at the adjacent Old State House -- a white Greek Revival building where Clinton planned to claim victory.
For Arkansans, Clinton's expected repeat of a feat no Democrat managed since Franklin Roosevelt was re-elected in 1944 represented a rehabilitation of sorts.

They had watched in dismay as the image of their state took a beating from the Whitewater financial imbroglio and other scandals that brought disaster to many native sons who accompanied Clinton to Washington after he wrested the White House from President George Bush in 1992.

The list of Arkansas casualties during Clinton's first term was long and grim -- deputy White House counsel Vince Foster, a Clinton friend from kindergarten, killed himself; Assistant Attorney General Webb Hubbell, a onetime law partner of Hillary Rodham Clinton, went to jail; and several other Friends of Bill, including former Surgeon General Joycelyn Elders, were sacked.

But those dark memories were being dispelled as the former governor stood poised for re-election. A Democratic official told Reuters Clinton's final internal poll showed him winning 47.2 percent of the vote and Dole getting 37.8 percent.
The poll showed Perot with 7.1 percent of the vote, and 7.1 percent was undecided, the official said.

Clinton, accompanied by his wife, Hillary, and their 16- year-old daughter, Chelsea, cast his paper ballot at a renovated train station on the edge of downtown Little Rock, two blocks from the state capitol building.
As he emerged back into the bright sunlight after voting, Clinton hugged and kissed Chelsea and exchanged a joyous high-five handslap with his daughter before entering his limousine and driving away.
The Clintons had arrived in their hometown aboard Air Force One in the early hours of Tuesday morning, closing out a grueling campaign season that unofficially began more than a year ago.
Their emotional return to a state Clinton led as governor for 12 years followed a late-night rally in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, the last stop on a 20-hour, six-state barnstorming finish.
"This is the greatest country in human history because we have created a system in which you are the boss," Clinton said in asking voters to renew his contract for four more years.
Enroute to Little Rock from South Dakota, the president and first lady toasted their staff and Secret Service agents who have been away from home so often because of the campaign.

Clinton and his aides also danced the Macarena, a popular Latin line dance that Democrats have adopted as a celebratory war dance. Asked to evaluate the commander-in-chief's performance, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had danced "in a presidential manner."

As the election returns came in, attention focused on the people who will surround Clinton for the next four years. White House chief of staff Ledon Panetta is among those departing -- he wants to go home to California and perhaps run for governor there in 1996.
Former Small Business Administration chief Erskine Bowles leads the list of possible replacements, but is resisting Clinton's entreaties to return to government service, White House sources said.
Secretary of State Warren Christopher, one of many cabinet officers in Little Rock for the anticipated victory party, was also expected to step down.

Sources said former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell, U.N. ambassador Madeleine Albright and former assistant Secretary of State Richard Holbrooke, who brokered the Bosnia peace agreement, were on the short list of contenders for Christopher's job.
